newsitem.title: USA: Motorola says charges possible in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Motorola says charges possible in 1997.

text.p: Motorola Inc said on Monday it would continue to take steps to restore the company's growth in profits and revenues which may result in charges against earnings later in 1997.
"We are continuing to vigorously pursue our program to improve financial performance," Christopher Galvin, chief executive of Motorola, said in a statement.

Motorola reported 1997 first quarter earnings of $325 million or $0.53 a share, down from the $384 million or $0.63 in the same quarter a year ago, but up from $238 million or $0.39 earned in the 1996 fourth quarter.

"This includes implementing cost reductions in businesses that are not achieving adequate profitability, reviewing development programs that have not lived up to their promise, and concentrating resources on technologies and geographic regions where we can establish or continue leadership," Galvin said. "These processes may result in decisions requiring unusual charges later in 1997."

Galvin said the global economic outlook continues promising, especially in emerging markets in Latin America and Asia. "Demand for our communications products and systems is strong in these markets. We see great opportunity for improved business in the developed world as well," he said.
"We are committed to restoring Motorola's long-term pattern of growth in profits and revenues," Galvin said.
Motorola's five percent decline in 1997 first quarter sales to $6.6 billion came largely from its semiconductor business, said Robert Growney, president.

While semiconductor sales and orders were lower than first quarter 1996 levels, orders improved from fourth quarter 1996 as the business emerged from last year's semiconductor industry recession, he said. "Steps taken in several business segments last year to reduce costs are beginning to have a favorable impact," he said in a statement.

During the 1997 first quarter, Motorola said the initial launch of global communications satellites under the Iridium project, originally scheduled for January 1997, was delayed as a result of a failed Delta II rocket launch unrelated to the Iridium program.
Motorola said it currently expects the first launch of Iridium satellites to occur in early May 1997.
As previously reported, Iridium LLC will require additional funding, possibly by late May 1997, to continue to make contractual payments to Motorola.

An agreement in principle has been reached with Iridium LLC to increase Motorola's guarantee of Iridium LLC bank financing by an additional $350 million to a new total of $1.1 billion, and Iridium LLC is also pursuing other funding options. There can be no assurances as to the availability to Iridium LLC of these funding options, Motorola said.
Galvin said he expects the Iridium launch to be resolved in the near future, and remains confident about the potential of the system.

While the initial launch of satellites has been delayed, Iridium LLC still expects to report higher depreciation expenses during the satellite deployment phase of the program. This will have an impact on Motorola financial results, although the impact will be somewhat less in 1997 than earlier expected, he said.
